book.Title: {{W|On the Founding of Places}}
book.page:
{{C|Of the Basin}}
If you mean to found by our custom, you will want a founder's basin. It is a shallow tin thing of no particular worth, kept by traders who deal in rope, salt, and other unglamorous necessities. Another vessel may serve a private sharing, but our charter-rite requires the basin: it is wide, and everyone can see into it.
Fill it with fresh water — eight drams is the customary measure, being enough that the pouring is felt — and set it down on ground you mean to keep. Then pour, and name the place aloud, and drink with whoever is standing there.
Our charter records that exact ground as claimed from that moment: not as a law above villages, freeholds, or water barons, but as a pledge made by sharing water before witnesses.

{{C|What Follows, and in What Order}}
In the settlements whose accounts I keep, the useful order is this.
{{W|First, beds.}} Settlers walk a long way on rumor. If there is nowhere to sleep when they arrive, they may look at your ground, think about their feet, and keep walking. Our charter counts room for no resident without a sound bed.
{{W|Second, water held.}} Not water passing through — water {{C|kept}}. A settlement following our rule is measured by what it can store against a dry month. Casks, then a cistern. Dedicate them openly, so the water-keepers know which vessels belong to the settlement and which are merely someone's.
{{W|Third, hands.}} A mill with nobody at it is a pile of good timber. Count your willing people before you commission the works, or expect those works to stand idle.

{{C|A Warning, Cheerfully Given}}
A lasting hearth is likely to be noticed.
Some who notice may want to trade with you. Some may demand payment not to trouble you. A few may simply come. None of these responses proves your rule a failure; each asks what kind of place you mean to keep.
Pay the tribute if the tribute is cheaper than the raid. Write down what happens either way. People, walls, and records each endure differently, but a careful account may speak after its clerk is gone.
